title: Policies, processes, procedures, and practices across the organization related to the mapping, measuring, and managing of AI risks are in place, transparent, and implemented effectively.
official: The organization sets up clear, written rules for how AI risks get spotted, measured, and handled, and makes sure everyone actually follows them.
metaphor: Posting the house rules on the fridge (no strangers inside, lock up at night) so everyone knows them and actually follows them, not just a list nobody reads.
translation: Write down simple, plain rules for how your household or small business will handle AI tools, put them somewhere everyone can see, and make sure people really use them.

title: Accountability structures are in place so that the appropriate teams and individuals are empowered, responsible, and trained for mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks.
official: Specific people are given the authority, the responsibility, and the training to handle AI risks, so it is always clear who owns each job.
metaphor: Deciding who in the family takes out the trash, who walks the dog, and who checks the smoke alarms, so nothing gets forgotten because everyone assumed someone else had it.
translation: Name who is in charge of the AI tools you use, give them the say-so and the know-how to do it, so it is never a mystery who is supposed to handle a problem.

title: Workforce diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility processes are prioritized in the mapping, measuring, and managing of AI risks throughout the lifecycle.
official: A mix of different people and viewpoints is deliberately included when weighing AI risks, so blind spots get caught that one narrow group would miss.
metaphor: Asking everyone at the dinner table, kids and grandparents included, before picking a family vacation, because each person notices problems the others would overlook.
translation: Bring in a range of voices (different ages, backgrounds, and needs) when you judge how an AI tool might help or harm people, since one point of view always misses something.

title: Organizational teams are committed to a culture that considers and communicates AI risk.
official: The whole group builds a habit of thinking about AI risks and talking about them openly, rather than staying quiet when something seems off.
metaphor: A household where anyone can say 'I smell gas' without being brushed off, so worries get spoken out loud instead of bottled up until something goes wrong.
translation: Build a habit where people feel safe raising concerns about AI tools out loud, so problems get talked about early instead of hidden until they blow up.

title: Processes are in place for robust engagement with relevant AI actors.
official: There are real channels for gathering input from the people affected by an AI system, including those who use it and those it makes decisions about.
metaphor: Holding a neighborhood meeting before putting up a big fence, so the people living next door get a genuine say instead of finding out after it is built.
translation: Set up ways to hear from the people your AI tool touches, like customers or staff, and take their feedback in before and after you roll it out.

title: Policies and procedures are in place to address AI risks and benefits arising from third-party software and data and other supply chain issues.
official: The organization has rules for handling the risks that come from AI tools and data built by outside vendors, not just the parts it made itself.
metaphor: Checking that the babysitter and the food delivery service you hire are trustworthy, because a stranger you let into the house is still your responsibility.
translation: Have a plan for the AI tools and data you buy or borrow from other companies, since a weakness in someone else's product can still become your problem.

title: Context is established and understood.
official: Before doing anything else, the team pins down where and why the AI system will be used and who it will affect, setting the stage for every later decision.
metaphor: Before rearranging the furniture, walking through the whole room to see where the doors, outlets, and walkways are, so the plan fits the space you actually have.
translation: Start by understanding exactly what job the AI tool is for, where it will be used, and who it will touch, so every choice after that makes sense for your situation.

title: Categorization of the AI system is performed.
official: The AI system is clearly labeled by what it does and how it works, so its risks can be judged against the right yardstick.
metaphor: Sorting the stuff in your garage into 'tools', 'sharp things', and 'flammable', because you store and handle each pile differently once you know what it is.
translation: Figure out what kind of AI tool you are dealing with and what it actually does, so you can size up its risks against the right expectations.

title: AI capabilities, targeted usage, goals, and expected benefits and costs compared with appropriate benchmarks are understood.
official: The team is honest about what the AI can and cannot do and weighs the expected payoff against the expected cost using sensible comparisons.
metaphor: Reading the real reviews and the price tag before buying a fancy blender, so you know what it can actually do and whether it is worth the money.
translation: Be clear-eyed about what the AI tool can really do, what you hope to gain, and what it will cost you, then check that the benefit is worth the trouble.

title: Risks and benefits are mapped for all components of the AI system including third-party software and data.
official: Every piece of the AI system, including the outside parts, gets its risks and benefits listed out so nothing important is left unexamined.
metaphor: Doing a full walk-around of a used car, tires, brakes, and engine, not just the shiny paint, so you spot the trouble before you buy.
translation: List the good and the risky parts of every piece of your AI tool, including the bits made by other companies, so nothing gets a free pass.

title: Impacts to individuals, groups, communities, organizations, and society are characterized.
official: The team thinks through how the AI system could affect real people and the wider world, not just the organization running it.
metaphor: Before starting a loud home renovation, thinking about how the noise and dust will hit not just your family but the neighbors up and down the street.
translation: Think through who could be helped or hurt by your AI tool, from single people to whole communities, so surprises to others do not blindside you later.

title: Appropriate methods and metrics are identified and applied.
official: The team picks the right tests and measurements for the AI system's risks and then actually runs them, instead of guessing.
metaphor: Using a real thermometer and a timer to cook the turkey, rather than poking it and hoping, so you actually know when it is done.
translation: Choose sensible ways to test and measure how your AI tool is doing, then use them, so you are working from facts instead of gut feeling.

title: AI systems are evaluated for trustworthy characteristics.
official: The AI system is checked against the marks of trustworthy AI, such as being safe, fair, private, secure, and understandable.
metaphor: Test-driving a car for brakes, steering, and blind spots before trusting it on the highway, not just admiring how it looks in the driveway.
translation: Actually test whether your AI tool is safe, fair, private, and understandable before you lean on it, instead of assuming it is fine.

title: Mechanisms for tracking identified AI risks over time are in place.
official: There are ongoing ways to keep an eye on known AI risks as time passes, so a small problem does not quietly grow worse.
metaphor: Keeping a chart on the wall for a slow leak under the sink, checking it weekly, so you notice if the drip is getting worse before the floor rots.
translation: Set up a way to keep watching the AI risks you already know about, so you catch a problem that is slowly getting bigger before it becomes a crisis.

title: Feedback about efficacy of measurement is gathered and assessed.
official: The team asks whether their tests and measurements are actually working and adjusts them based on what they learn.
metaphor: Noticing your bathroom scale reads five pounds off, then recalibrating it, because a measuring tool you never double-check can quietly mislead you.
translation: Check that your ways of testing the AI tool are truly telling you the truth, and fix them if they are not, so you are not fooled by bad measurements.

title: AI risks based on assessments and other analytical output from the MAP and MEASURE functions are prioritized, responded to, and managed.
official: Using everything learned so far, the team ranks the AI risks by importance and takes real action on the ones that matter most.
metaphor: After a home inspection lists ten issues, fixing the broken furnace first and the squeaky door last, because you tackle the dangerous stuff before the annoyances.
translation: Take what you learned about your AI tool's risks, put them in order of how serious they are, and deal with the biggest ones first.

title: Strategies to maximize AI benefits and minimize negative impacts are planned, prepared, implemented, documented, and informed by input from relevant AI actors.
official: The team plans and carries out steps to get the most good and the least harm from the AI system, writing it down and shaping it with input from those involved.
metaphor: Planning a road trip to hit the best stops while avoiding the toll roads and traffic, writing the route down, and asking passengers what they want along the way.
translation: Make and follow a written plan to get the most benefit and the least harm from your AI tool, and let the people involved help shape that plan.

title: AI risks and benefits from third-party entities are managed.
official: The risks and rewards coming from outside vendors' AI tools and data are actively handled, not just noticed once and forgotten.
metaphor: Staying on top of the contractor you hired for the roof, checking their work and keeping their number handy, rather than paying up front and hoping for the best.
translation: Keep actively managing the AI tools and data you get from other companies, checking on them over time instead of trusting them once and walking away.

title: Risk treatments, including response and recovery, and communication plans for the identified and measured AI risks are documented and monitored regularly.
official: The steps for responding to and recovering from AI problems, plus who to tell, are written down and checked on a regular basis so they stay ready.
metaphor: Keeping a fire escape plan and a list of emergency numbers on the fridge, then running a drill now and then, so nobody freezes up when something actually happens.
translation: Write down how you will respond to and recover from an AI problem and who you will notify, then review it regularly so the plan is ready when you need it.

title: Prompt Injection
official: Crafted user input or hidden text alters an LLM's behavior or output in ways the designers did not intend, whether the manipulation is directly typed or buried in content the model reads.
metaphor: A stranger tucking a fake note into your kid's lunchbox that tells the babysitter to unlock the front door.
translation: Attackers hide sneaky instructions in the words an AI reads, tricking it into ignoring its rules and doing things you never asked for.

title: Sensitive Information Disclosure
official: An LLM reveals private data, secrets, or proprietary details through its responses, either because that information was in its training or because it was fed in during a conversation.
metaphor: A chatty house guest who repeats your bank PIN and home address to whoever asks over dinner.
translation: The AI can accidentally blurt out private information (passwords, personal records, company secrets) to people who should never see it.

title: Supply Chain
official: Weaknesses enter through the outside pieces an LLM depends on, such as third-party models, training datasets, and software libraries, any of which can be tampered with or poorly vetted.
metaphor: Building your house with lumber and locks from a stranger's truck, never checking whether any of it is rotten or rigged.
translation: AI systems are assembled from borrowed models, data, and code; if any of those outside parts is tampered with or flawed, the whole system inherits the problem.

title: Data and Model Poisoning
official: Attackers corrupt the data used to train or fine-tune a model, planting biases, backdoors, or flaws that quietly shape how the model behaves later.
metaphor: Someone slipping bad ingredients into the flour bin so every loaf your family bakes for months comes out tainted.
translation: If the examples an AI learns from are secretly rigged, the finished model carries hidden flaws or backdoors that show up long after training.

title: Improper Output Handling
official: An application trusts and forwards an LLM's output without validating or cleaning it first, letting whatever the model produced flow straight into other systems and cause harm.
metaphor: Letting your kid read a mystery text message aloud and acting on it instantly, without ever checking who really sent it.
translation: When software blindly trusts whatever the AI spits out and passes it along unchecked, malicious content can slip through and damage other systems.

title: Excessive Agency
official: An LLM is handed too much power, too many tools, or too broad a set of permissions, so a bad decision or a hijacked prompt can trigger real-world actions well beyond what was needed.
metaphor: Giving the house-sitter the keys to your car, your safe, and your bank account when all they needed was to feed the cat.
translation: When an AI is allowed to take actions and touch systems far beyond its job, a single mistake or manipulation can cause outsized real-world damage.

title: System Prompt Leakage
official: The hidden setup instructions that govern an LLM get exposed, revealing rules, secrets, or logic that were meant to stay behind the scenes and can then be exploited.
metaphor: Leaving the babysitter's private instruction sheet, including the alarm code, taped to the front window for anyone to read.
translation: The behind-the-scenes rules that guide an AI can leak out, and once attackers see those instructions they can find the gaps and work around them.

title: Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
official: Flaws in how a system generates, stores, or retrieves the numeric representations behind retrieval-augmented generation let attackers poison the knowledge store or pull out information they should not access.
metaphor: A home filing cabinet with a broken lock, where anyone can slip in fake documents or read the family's private folders.
translation: AI systems that look up stored knowledge can be attacked through that memory bank, letting bad actors plant false facts or steal what is filed there.

title: Misinformation
official: An LLM produces false or fabricated statements that sound convincing, and people relying on the system act on that wrong information as if it were true.
metaphor: A know-it-all neighbor who confidently gives you wrong directions, so you drive an hour the wrong way trusting them.
translation: AI can state made-up or incorrect facts in a confident tone, and if you trust it without checking, you end up acting on things that simply are not true.

title: Unbounded Consumption
official: An LLM is allowed to run without sensible limits, so attackers can flood it with heavy requests that drain computing resources, run up costs, or knock the service offline.
metaphor: A guest who leaves every faucet and the garden hose running all day, spiking your water bill until the tank runs dry.
translation: Without caps on how much work an AI will do, attackers can overload it with expensive requests, racking up huge bills or crashing the service for everyone.

title: Reconnaissance
official: The adversary gathers information about a target's AI systems to plan later operations, using techniques such as Search Open Technical Databases, Search Open AI Vulnerability Analysis, and Active Scanning.
metaphor: Casing a house from the sidewalk before a break-in: noting which doors have locks, where the cameras point, and when the family leaves for work.
translation: Before attacking an AI system, adversaries study it: what model it runs, how it was built, any publicly reported weaknesses, and where its soft spots are.

title: Resource Development
official: The adversary builds, buys, or steals the resources needed to support an attack, using techniques such as Acquire Public AI Artifacts, Develop Capabilities, and Publish Poisoned Datasets.
metaphor: A burglar assembling a kit before the job: buying lock picks, copying a key, and parking a getaway van a block away.
translation: Attackers set up their toolkit: grabbing public models and datasets, writing malware, renting servers and accounts, or seeding tampered data for later use.

title: Initial Access
official: The adversary tries to gain a first foothold in the AI system, using techniques such as AI Supply Chain Compromise, Valid Accounts, and Exploit Public-Facing Application.
metaphor: Getting through the front door the first time: a stolen key, an unlocked window, or a tampered package left on the porch.
translation: Attackers find a way in: poisoning the AI supply chain, stealing valid logins, phishing staff, or exploiting an internet-facing application.

title: AI Model Access
official: The adversary seeks some level of access to the AI model itself, using techniques such as AI Model Inference API Access, AI-Enabled Product or Service, and Full AI Model Access.
metaphor: Getting close to the safe: peering through the keyhole, using it as a paying customer, or holding the full combination and its internal workings.
translation: Attackers get their hands on the model, from simply querying its API to fully accessing its internals, so they can probe it, feed it data, and craft attacks.

title: Execution
official: The adversary tries to run malicious code or instructions on the system, using techniques such as LLM Prompt Injection, User Execution, and AI Agent Tool Invocation.
metaphor: Tricking someone inside the house into carrying out your orders, like slipping a fake instruction into the family's chore list.
translation: Attackers get the AI system to run their code or hidden instructions, for example by smuggling commands into a prompt that an LLM or agent then obeys.

title: Persistence
official: The adversary tries to keep their foothold across restarts and cleanups, using techniques such as Poison Training Data, Manipulate AI Model, and RAG Poisoning.
metaphor: Hiding a spare key under the mat so you can slip back in even after the family changes the locks.
translation: Attackers plant lasting backdoors in the AI: poisoned training data, a tampered model, or corrupted knowledge sources, so they keep access after reboots and fixes.

title: Privilege Escalation
official: The adversary tries to gain higher-level permissions, using techniques such as LLM Jailbreak, AI Agent Tool Invocation, and Escape to Host.
metaphor: A guest let into the living room finding the master key and quietly unlocking every other room in the house.
translation: Attackers turn limited access into broad control: jailbreaking an LLM past its guardrails, abusing an agent's tools, or breaking out onto the host machine.

title: Defense Evasion
official: The adversary tries to avoid detection by AI-enabled defenses, using techniques such as Evade AI Model, LLM Prompt Obfuscation, and LLM Jailbreak.
metaphor: Wearing a disguise and stepping around the security cameras so the guard dog never barks.
translation: Attackers dodge AI-based detection: crafting inputs that slip past malware or content filters, or disguising prompts so the model never flags them.

title: Credential Access
official: The adversary tries to steal account names and passwords, using techniques such as Unsecured Credentials, RAG Credential Harvesting, and Credentials from AI Agent Configuration.
metaphor: Rifling through the kitchen drawers for the sticky note where someone wrote down all the passwords.
translation: Attackers hunt for logins and keys, pulling secrets out of AI agent configs, knowledge bases, or carelessly stored credentials to unlock more of the system.

title: Discovery
official: The adversary tries to map the AI environment from the inside, using techniques such as Discover AI Model Family, Discover AI Artifacts, and Discover LLM System Information.
metaphor: Once inside, wandering room to room to learn the layout: where the valuables sit and which doors lead where.
translation: Now inside, attackers explore the AI setup: which model family it is, what data and artifacts exist, and how it is configured, to plan their next move.

title: Lateral Movement
official: The adversary tries to move through the AI environment to reach other systems, using techniques such as Use Alternate Authentication Material and Phishing.
metaphor: Having slipped into one room, using a found keycard to move down the hall into the offices and storage closets.
translation: Attackers pivot from their entry point to other systems, like model registries, notebooks, or training pipelines, often reusing stolen keys or hijacking over-privileged AI agents.

title: Collection
official: The adversary gathers the AI artifacts and data relevant to their goal, using techniques such as AI Artifact Collection, Data from Information Repositories, and Data from AI Services.
metaphor: Going through the house and piling everything worth taking, jewelry, documents, electronics, by the back door.
translation: Attackers scoop up the valuable material: models, training data, and files from repositories, local systems, and AI services, staging it to steal or reuse.

title: AI Attack Staging
official: The adversary prepares and tunes the attack on the target model, using techniques such as Create Proxy AI Model, Craft Adversarial Data, and Verify Attack.
metaphor: Buying the exact same lock as your target and practicing on it at home until you can pick it in seconds.
translation: Attackers rehearse offline: building a copycat model, crafting tricky inputs, or tampering with the model, then verifying the attack works before firing it for real.

title: Command and Control
official: The adversary tries to communicate with and remotely control compromised AI systems, using techniques such as Reverse Shell, AI Service API, and AI Agent.
metaphor: A burglar leaving a walkie-talkie hidden inside so an accomplice outside can quietly relay orders.
translation: Attackers set up a hidden channel to steer a compromised AI system from afar, often disguising the traffic as ordinary API calls or normal agent activity.

title: Exfiltration
official: The adversary tries to steal AI artifacts and other data, using techniques such as Exfiltration via AI Inference API, Extract LLM System Prompt, and LLM Data Leakage.
metaphor: Carrying the loot out of the house, whether stuffed in a backpack or smuggled out little by little with the trash.
translation: Attackers spirit data out: model weights, training data, or secrets, by coaxing an LLM to leak its prompt or answers, or by channeling data through the inference API.

title: Impact
official: The adversary tries to manipulate, disrupt, erode confidence in, or destroy AI systems and data, using techniques such as Denial of AI Service, Erode AI Model Integrity, and Cost Harvesting.
metaphor: Trashing the house on the way out: smashing things, jamming the locks, and running up the utility bills out of spite.
translation: Attackers cause the real damage: knocking the AI offline, degrading its accuracy, running up huge compute bills, or using its outputs to harm people and erode trust.

title: What ISO/IEC 42001 is
official: ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable international standard that lays out how to build and run a management system for governing artificial intelligence responsibly, using the same repeatable structure shared by other ISO management standards.
metaphor: A recipe book for running a safe household kitchen: not the individual dishes, but the routines for who cooks, how you check ingredients, and how you keep everyone from getting sick.
translation: An organization adopts a structured, risk-based program for governing its AI, and can have an outside auditor certify that the program actually works, instead of just promising that it does.

title: Context of the organization
official: This part asks the organization to map the internal and external factors, the people affected, and the boundaries that decide what its AI management system needs to cover.
metaphor: Before setting house rules, you take stock of who lives here, who visits, what the neighborhood is like, and which rooms the rules will actually apply to.
translation: The organization writes down why it uses AI, who is affected by it, and exactly which AI systems and activities fall inside the program's scope.

title: Leadership and AI policy
official: Senior leaders must own the AI program, publish a clear AI policy, and assign named roles so responsibility for AI decisions is never left vague.
metaphor: The parents set the household's rules on screens and safety, post them on the fridge, and make clear who decides what, instead of letting everyone freelance.
translation: Top management approves an AI policy, backs it with real resources, and names who is accountable, so AI choices are deliberate rather than ad hoc.

title: Planning and AI risk
official: The organization identifies what could go wrong with its AI, decides which risks matter most, plans how to treat them, and sets measurable objectives to steer the program.
metaphor: Childproofing the house before the baby crawls: you walk room to room spotting hazards, decide which to fix first, and plan the safety gates and outlet covers.
translation: The organization runs an AI risk assessment, chooses treatments for the risks it finds, and sets concrete goals so the plan can be tracked over time.

title: Support: people, skills, and records
official: This covers the everyday resources that keep the program alive: budget and tools, trained and aware staff, clear communication, and well kept documentation.
metaphor: A working household kitchen needs stocked cupboards, someone who knows how to cook, everyone told about the peanut allergy, and labeled leftovers so nothing is a mystery.
translation: The organization funds the program, trains and informs its people, communicates clearly, and keeps its records current so decisions can be shown later.

title: Operation and AI impact assessment
official: This is where plans become daily practice: the organization runs its AI controls, manages each system across its lifecycle, and assesses how that AI could affect individuals and society.
metaphor: Actually cooking dinner every night while following the safety routines, and pausing to think about how a new dish might affect guests with allergies or special diets.
translation: The organization operates its AI under the controls it planned and, before and during use, evaluates the real-world impact of each system on the people it touches.

title: Performance evaluation
official: The organization checks whether the program is working by monitoring and measuring it, running internal audits, and holding formal leadership reviews.
metaphor: The family periodically tests the smoke alarms, does a walk-through inspection, and sits down at dinner to ask whether the house rules are really keeping everyone safe.
translation: The organization measures how well its AI controls perform, audits itself, and has leaders formally review the results and decide what needs to change.

title: Improvement
official: When something falls short, the organization fixes the immediate problem, digs into the root cause, and keeps refining the program over time.
metaphor: After a small kitchen fire, you do not just put it out; you figure out why it started and change the habit so it does not happen again.
translation: The organization corrects failures, addresses their underlying causes, and treats the AI program as something it continually tunes rather than sets once and forgets.

title: Annex A control themes
official: Annex A offers a reference menu of AI-specific safeguards grouped by theme, spanning policies, internal roles, resources, impact assessment, the system lifecycle, data handling, transparency to stakeholders, responsible use, and third-party arrangements.
metaphor: A checklist of household safety measures to choose from: door locks, smoke alarms, a chore chart, labeling the cleaning chemicals, teaching the kids the rules, and vetting the babysitter.
translation: The organization selects from a catalog of AI safeguards, justifying which ones apply, to cover data quality, transparency, human oversight, and control of outside vendors.
